statement: Let $f, g$ be [time-constructible](c:time-constructible-function) functions with $f(n)\log f(n) = o(g(n))$. Then $\mathrm{DTIME}(f(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{DTIME}(g(n))$: some language is decided by a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) in time $O(g(n))$ and by none in time $O(f(n))$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [time-constructible](c:time-constructible-function), so $f(n) \ge n$.
The function $g$ is [time-constructible](c:time-constructible-function): a machine writes $g(n)$ in time $O(g(n))$.
The growth gap holds: $f(n)\log f(n) = o(g(n))$ in [asymptotic notation](c:asymptotic-notation).

conclusion: The class $\mathrm{DTIME}(f(n))$ is a proper subset of $\mathrm{DTIME}(g(n))$.

proofs.name: Clocked diagonalization
proofs.slogan: Build a machine that runs in time $O(g)$ and does the opposite of every machine that runs in time $O(f)$ on that machine's own code.
proofs.scope: The proper inclusion; the inclusion $\mathrm{DTIME}(f) \subseteq \mathrm{DTIME}(g)$ is immediate because $f \le f \log f = o(g)$ eventually. Machines are deterministic, with codes that may be padded.

roles.why: It lets the machine $D$ count $g(|x|)$ steps and stop in time $O(g)$.
It gives $f(n) \ge n$, so simulating an $f$-time machine costs $O(f \log f)$.
The gap $f \log f = o(g)$ makes the simulation fit in the clock for long inputs.

steps.slogan: Define a machine $D$ that runs the machine coded by its input for $g(|x|)$ steps.
steps.detail: On input $x$, $D$ reads $x$ as the code of a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $M_x$ and starts a clock of $g(|x|)$ steps. Inside the clock a universal machine simulates $M_x$ on $x$. If the simulation ends with output $b$, then $D$ outputs $1 - b$; if the clock runs out, $D$ outputs $0$.

steps.slogan: Place the language of $D$ in $\mathrm{DTIME}(g(n))$.
steps.detail: The clock needs $O(g(|x|))$ steps, because $g$ is [time-constructible](c:time-constructible-function). Running the clock beside the simulation costs only a constant factor, so $D$ halts in time $O(g(n))$ on every input.

steps.slogan: Suppose that a machine $M$ decides the language of $D$ in time $c f(n)$.
steps.detail: Every machine has infinitely many codes, since a code can be padded with unused states. Let $x$ be a code of $M$ that is as long as we need.

steps.slogan: Show that the clock of $D$ outlasts the simulation of $M$ on a long code $x$.
steps.detail: A universal machine simulates $c f(|x|)$ steps of $M$ in time $c' c f(|x|)\log f(|x|)$, with $c'$ depending only on $M$. Because $f \log f = o(g)$, this is less than $g(|x|)$ once $|x|$ is large, so $D$ finishes the simulation.

steps.slogan: Compare $D(x)$ with $M(x)$ to reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: By the last step $D(x) = 1 - M(x) \neq M(x)$, so $M$ does not decide the language of $D$. This contradicts the choice of $M$, so no machine in time $O(f)$ decides it, and the language lies in $\mathrm{DTIME}(g) \setminus \mathrm{DTIME}(f)$.

concepts.c:time-constructible-function: Constructibility lets $D$ and the simulation use exact step counts.
concepts.c:turing-machine: Codes of machines are the inputs on which $D$ diagonalizes.
concepts.c:asymptotic-notation: Little-o says that the simulation cost is eventually below $g$.

source.note: The classical diagonal proof of Hartmanis and Stearns (1965), as in Arora and Barak, Computational Complexity, Theorem 3.1.

statement: Let $E$ be a [Banach space](c:banach-space), $F$ a normed space and $(T_i)_{i \in I}$ a family of [bounded linear operators](c:bounded-linear-operator) $E \to F$ with $\sup_i \|T_i x\| < \infty$ for each $x \in E$. Then $\sup_i \|T_i\| < \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space).
Each $T_i\colon E \to F$ is a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) into a normed space $F$.
For each $x \in E$ the set $\{\|T_i x\| : i \in I\}$ is bounded.

conclusion: A constant $C$ exists with $\|T_i\| \le C$ for every $i \in I$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows seminormed spaces and semilinear maps between nontrivially normed fields, with $E$ complete. Its conclusion is the same uniform bound on the norms of the maps.

proofs.name: Baire category
proofs.slogan: Cover the space by the closed sets where all values stay below $n$, find a ball in one of them, and move it to the origin.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for $E \neq \{0\}$ ($E = \{0\}$ gives all norms zero). The constant obtained is $C = 4n/r$ for the ball found in step 2.

roles.why: It makes the closed sets $A_n$ cover $E$.
Continuity makes each $A_n$ closed, and linearity transfers a bound from a ball to every vector.
Completeness makes $E$ a [Baire space](c:baire-space), so one set $A_n$ has interior.

steps.slogan: Cover $E$ by the sets $A_n$ where every $\|T_i x\|$ is at most $n$.
steps.detail: Put $A_n = \bigcap_i \{x : \|T_i x\| \le n\}$. Each $A_n$ is an intersection of preimages of a [closed set](c:closed-set) under continuous maps, so it is closed. By pointwise boundedness every $x$ lies in some $A_n$, so $E = \bigcup_n A_n$.

steps.slogan: Find a ball inside one set $A_n$ by the Baire category theorem.
steps.detail: A [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) is a [Baire space](c:baire-space), so a countable union of closed sets covering $E$ has a member with nonempty interior. Hence some $A_n$ contains a ball $B(x_0, r)$.

steps.slogan: Translate the ball to the origin to bound every $T_i$ on a ball around $0$.
steps.detail: Since $x_0 \in A_n$ and $x_0 + y \in A_n$ for $\|y\| < r$, we get $\|T_i y\| = \|T_i(x_0 + y) - T_i x_0\| \le 2n$ for all $i$ and all $\|y\| < r$.

steps.slogan: Scale an arbitrary vector into the ball to bound the [operator norm](c:operator-norm).
steps.detail: For $x \neq 0$ put $y = \frac{r}{2}\,x/\|x\|$. Linearity gives $\|T_i x\| = \frac{2\|x\|}{r}\|T_i y\| \le \frac{4n}{r}\|x\|$. So $\|T_i\| \le 4n/r$ for every $i$.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness is the hypothesis that the Baire category theorem needs.
concepts.c:bounded-linear-operator: The operators are continuous and linear, which the covering and scaling steps use.
concepts.c:baire-space: A Baire space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness of the metric is what makes the space a Baire space.
concepts.c:closed-set: Closedness of the sets $A_n$ lets Baire's theorem apply.
concepts.c:operator-norm: The operator norm is the quantity that the proof bounds uniformly.

source.note: mathlib proves that a Baire space is barrelled (BaireSpace.instBarrelledSpace) by this closed-cover, translate and double argument, and applies it to the supremum seminorm (WithSeminorms.banach_steinhaus).

proofs.name: Inductive choice of signs
proofs.slogan: Build a point by choosing signs along a sparse sequence of operators, and show that the values of those operators blow up.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, without the Baire category theorem. It argues by contradiction from $\sup_i \|T_i\| = \infty$.

roles.why: Linearity gives the key inequality, and finite norms give vectors that nearly attain them.
Completeness makes the series of small steps converge to a point $x$.
It contradicts the blow-up of $\|T_n x\|$ at the limit point.

steps.slogan: Show that one of $x \pm \xi$ gives $T$ a value at least as large as $T\xi$.
steps.detail: For a linear $T$ and vectors $x, \xi$, we have $2T\xi = T(x + \xi) - T(x - \xi)$. So $\max(\|T(x+\xi)\|, \|T(x-\xi)\|) \ge \|T\xi\|$.

steps.slogan: Assume that the norms are unbounded and pick operators $T_n$ with $\|T_n\| \ge 4^n$.
steps.detail: If $\sup_i \|T_i\| = \infty$, then for each $n \ge 1$ some $T_n$ in the family has $\|T_n\| \ge 4^n$. We show that this contradicts pointwise boundedness.

steps.slogan: Choose points $x_n = x_{n-1} \pm \xi_n$ so that $\|T_n x_n\|$ is large.
steps.detail: Let $x_0 = 0$. Pick $\xi_n$ with $\|\xi_n\| \le 3^{-n}$ and $\|T_n \xi_n\| \ge \frac23 3^{-n}\|T_n\|$. By the key inequality choose the sign so that $\|T_n x_n\| \ge \|T_n \xi_n\|$.

steps.slogan: Take the limit $x$ of the points $x_n$ in the complete space.
steps.detail: Since $\sum \|\xi_n\| \le \sum 3^{-n} < \infty$ and $E$ is complete, the sequence $x_n$ converges to some $x$. The tail satisfies $\|x - x_n\| \le \sum_{k > n} 3^{-k} = 3^{-n}/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\|T_n x\|$ tends to infinity, which contradicts pointwise boundedness.
steps.detail: We have $\|T_n x\| \ge \|T_n x_n\| - \|T_n\|\,\|x - x_n\| \ge (\frac23 - \frac12)3^{-n}\|T_n\| \ge \frac16 (4/3)^n \to \infty$. This contradicts the bound on $\{\|T_i x\|\}$.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness gives the limit of the constructed sequence.
concepts.c:bounded-linear-operator: Each operator has a finite norm and is linear.

source.note: A. D. Sokal, A really simple elementary proof of the uniform boundedness theorem, American Mathematical Monthly 118 (2011).

statement: Let $v$ be a $C^1$ [vector field](c:vector-field) on a Hausdorff [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$. If $\gamma, \gamma'\colon (a, b) \to M$ are integral curves of $v$ with $\gamma(t_0) = \gamma'(t_0)$ for some $t_0 \in (a, b)$, then $\gamma = \gamma'$ on $(a, b)$.

hypotheses.text: The [vector field](c:vector-field) $v$ is $C^1$.
The manifold $M$ is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
The maps $\gamma, \gamma'$ are differentiable and satisfy $\dot\gamma = v \circ \gamma$ and $\dot\gamma' = v \circ \gamma'$ on $(a, b)$.
The curves agree at one time: $\gamma(t_0) = \gamma'(t_0)$ with $t_0 \in (a, b)$.

conclusion: The two curves are equal at every time of $(a, b)$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows manifolds modelled on any real normed space, possibly infinite dimensional, with a $C^1$ structure and no boundary. The Hausdorff hypothesis is the declaration's T2 assumption.

proofs.name: Clopen agreement set
proofs.slogan: Show that the set of times where the curves agree is nonempty, closed and open, then use the connectedness of the interval.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on an open interval; the interval may be unbounded. Openness is the local uniqueness theorem for ODEs in one chart.

roles.why: It puts $t_0$ in the agreement set, so the set is nonempty.
Continuity of the curves makes the set closed, and the equations $\dot\gamma = v \circ \gamma$ give the chart equation.
In a Hausdorff space the diagonal is closed, which closes the agreement set.
A $C^1$ field has a locally Lipschitz chart expression, which feeds Grönwall's inequality.

steps.slogan: Collect the times where the two curves agree into a set $S$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \{t \in (a, b) : \gamma(t) = \gamma'(t)\}$. The point $t_0$ lies in $S$, so $S$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ is closed in $(a, b)$.
steps.detail: The map $t \mapsto (\gamma(t), \gamma'(t))$ is continuous, and the diagonal of $M \times M$ is closed because $M$ is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space). So $S$, the preimage of the diagonal, is closed.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ is open by comparing both curves in one chart.
steps.detail: Let $t_1 \in S$ and take a chart $\varphi$ at $\gamma(t_1)$. Near $t_1$ both $\varphi\circ\gamma$ and $\varphi\circ\gamma'$ solve $x' = V(x)$, where $V$ is the $C^1$ chart expression of $v$, hence [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) with some constant $K$. Then $u = |\varphi\gamma - \varphi\gamma'|$ obeys $u(t) \le K\bigl|\int_{t_1}^t u\bigr|$ with $u(t_1) = 0$, so $u = 0$ near $t_1$ by Grönwall's lemma.

steps.slogan: Conclude from the connectedness of the interval that $S = (a, b)$.
steps.detail: The set $S$ is nonempty, closed and open in $(a, b)$, so it is [clopen](c:clopen-subset). The interval is a [connected space](c:connected-space), so $S = (a, b)$.

concepts.c:vector-field: The field defines the equation that both curves solve.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Charts turn the equation on the manifold into an ODE on a vector space.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Hausdorff separation makes the set of agreement times closed.
concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: A Lipschitz chart field gives the estimate that Grönwall's lemma needs.
concepts.c:clopen-subset: The agreement set is both open and closed in the interval.
concepts.c:connected-space: A connected interval has no proper nonempty clopen subset.

source.note: mathlib proves local uniqueness in a chart with ODE_solution_unique_of_eventually (Grönwall), then shows the agreement set is clopen in the preconnected interval (isPreconnected_Ioo).

statement: Let $A$ be a [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring) with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and let $g = \sum a_i X^i \in A[[X]]$ have some coefficient outside $\mathfrak m$; let $n$ be the least such index. Then $g = f h$ with $f$ a [distinguished polynomial](c:is-distinguished-at) of degree $n$ and $h$ a unit of $A[[X]]$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $A$ is a [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring) with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$.
Some coefficient of the [power series](c:power-series) $g$ lies outside $\mathfrak m$.

conclusion: The series factors as $g = f h$, where $f = X^n + c_{n-1}X^{n-1} + \dots + c_0$ with all $c_j \in \mathfrak m$ and $h$ is a unit.

formal.difference: The declaration states the same factorization for a ring that is adically complete for its maximal ideal. The analytic theorem for convergent series over $\mathbb C$ is a separate result.

proofs.name: Weierstrass division of $X^n$
proofs.slogan: Divide $X^n$ by $g$ with a quotient and a remainder of degree below $n$, then read the factorization from that division.
proofs.scope: The whole formal theorem. The case $n = 0$ is included: then $g$ is a unit and $f = 1$.

roles.why: It defines $n$ and makes the tail of $g$ a unit, which is the divisor condition.
A non-member of $\mathfrak m$ is a unit, and completeness makes the geometric series converge.

steps.slogan: Split $g$ into a low part with coefficients in $\mathfrak m$ and a unit tail.
steps.detail: Write $g = \alpha + X^n u$ with $\alpha = \sum_{i<n} a_i X^i$ and $u = \sum_{i \ge n} a_i X^{i-n}$. The coefficients of $\alpha$ lie in $\mathfrak m$. The constant term $a_n \notin \mathfrak m$ is a unit of the [local ring](c:local-ring), so $u$ is a unit of $A[[X]]$.

steps.slogan: Turn the division of $X^n$ by $g$ into the equation $(1 + L)Q = 1$.
steps.detail: Let $\tau$ drop the first $n$ terms of a series and divide by $X^n$. If $X^n = qg + r$ with $r$ a polynomial of degree below $n$, then $\tau$ gives $1 = \tau(q\alpha) + qu$. With $Q = qu$ this reads $Q + L(Q) = 1$, where $L(Q) = \tau(Q u^{-1}\alpha)$ maps $\mathfrak m^k A[[X]]$ into $\mathfrak m^{k+1}A[[X]]$.

steps.slogan: Solve for $Q$ with the geometric series $\sum_k (-L)^k(1)$.
steps.detail: The $k$-th term lies in $\mathfrak m^k A[[X]]$, so each coefficient series converges because $A$ is complete. The sum $Q$ satisfies $(1+L)Q = 1$. Put $q = Qu^{-1}$ and $r = X^n - qg$; then $\tau(r) = 0$, so $r$ is a polynomial of degree below $n$.

steps.slogan: Reduce modulo $\mathfrak m$ to show that $q$ is a unit and $r$ has coefficients in $\mathfrak m$.
steps.detail: Modulo $\mathfrak m$ we have $\bar g = X^n\bar u$ and $X^n = \bar q X^n \bar u + \bar r$. So $X^n$ divides $\bar r$, which has degree below $n$; hence $\bar r = 0$ and $\bar q\bar u = 1$. Thus $q(0) \notin \mathfrak m$, so $q$ is a unit, and every coefficient of $r$ lies in $\mathfrak m$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the division as the factorization $g = f h$.
steps.detail: From $X^n = qg + r$ we get $g = q^{-1}(X^n - r)$. The polynomial $f = X^n - r$ is monic of degree $n$ with its lower coefficients in $\mathfrak m$, so it is [distinguished](c:is-distinguished-at), and $h = q^{-1}$ is a unit.

concepts.c:complete-local-ring: Completeness gives the limit; the local property makes non-members of $\mathfrak m$ units.
concepts.c:power-series: The factorization lives in the ring of power series over $A$.
concepts.c:local-ring: Elements outside the maximal ideal are units, so the tail $u$ is a unit.
concepts.c:is-distinguished-at: The factor $f$ is monic with all lower coefficients in $\mathfrak m$.

source.note: mathlib divides $X^n$ by $g$ (exists_isWeierstrassDivision, built from a limit of approximate quotients) and turns quotient and remainder into the factorization (IsWeierstrassDivision.isWeierstrassFactorization), after Washington, Introduction to Cyclotomic Fields, Theorem 7.3.

statement: For a [weighted sum](c:weighted-sum) over a finite index set $I$, a real $p \ge 1$ and nonnegative reals $w_i, f_i$: $\sum_i w_i f_i \le \bigl(\sum_i w_i\bigr)^{1 - 1/p}\bigl(\sum_i w_i f_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}$.

hypotheses.text: The exponent satisfies $p \ge 1$.
The weights $w_i$ and the values $f_i$ are nonnegative reals.
The index set $I$ is finite, so every sum is a [finite sum](c:finite-sum).

conclusion: The weighted sum $\sum_i w_i f_i$ is at most $\bigl(\sum_i w_i\bigr)^{1-1/p}\bigl(\sum_i w_i f_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the inequality for functions into the nonnegative reals on a finset of any index type. The versions for real and for extended-real values are separate declarations.

proofs.name: Hölder with a split weight
proofs.slogan: Write each term as a product of two powers of the weight and apply Hölder's inequality to the two factors.
proofs.scope: The case $p > 1$. For $p = 1$ both sides equal $\sum_i w_i f_i$, because the first exponent is $0$.

roles.why: Nonnegativity makes the real powers of $w_i$ and of $f_i$ defined and the factors nonnegative.
The value $p > 1$ gives the conjugate exponent $q = p/(p-1)$.
Hölder's inequality for finite sums applies to the finite index set.

steps.slogan: Factor each term as $w_i f_i = w_i^{1-1/p}\,(w_i^{1/p} f_i)$.
steps.detail: Because $w_i \ge 0$, the exponents add: $w_i^{1-1/p}\,w_i^{1/p} = w_i$. So $\sum_i w_i f_i = \sum_i u_i v_i$ with the nonnegative numbers $u_i = w_i^{1-1/p}$ and $v_i = w_i^{1/p} f_i$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\sum u_i v_i$ by Hölder's inequality with the [conjugate exponents](c:holder-conjugate-exponents) $q = p/(p-1)$ and $p$.
steps.detail: For $p > 1$ we have $1/q + 1/p = 1$. Hölder's inequality gives $\sum_i u_i v_i \le \bigl(\sum_i u_i^q\bigr)^{1/q}\bigl(\sum_i v_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}$.

steps.slogan: Simplify the powers to get the weighted form of the bound.
steps.detail: Since $(1 - 1/p)\,q = 1$, we have $u_i^q = w_i$, and $1/q = 1 - 1/p$. Also $v_i^p = w_i f_i^p$. Substituting gives $\sum_i w_i f_i \le \bigl(\sum_i w_i\bigr)^{1-1/p}\bigl(\sum_i w_i f_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}$.

concepts.c:weighted-sum: The left side is a sum of the values $f_i$ with weights $w_i$.
concepts.c:finite-sum: Hölder's inequality is applied to sums over a finite index set.
concepts.c:holder-conjugate-exponents: The exponents $q$ and $p$ satisfy $1/q + 1/p = 1$, as Hölder requires.

source.note: mathlib factors $w f$ as $w^{1-1/p}(w^{1/p} f)$, applies inner_le_Lp_mul_Lq with Hölder conjugate exponents, and simplifies the powers.

proofs.name: Jensen for the power function
proofs.slogan: Normalize the weights to a probability vector and apply Jensen's inequality to the convex function $t^p$.
proofs.scope: The case $p > 1$ and $\sum_i w_i > 0$. If all $w_i = 0$ both sides are $0$; for $p = 1$ both sides are equal.

roles.why: Nonnegative weights give a probability vector and keep the $p$-th root well defined.
The condition $p \ge 1$ makes $t \mapsto t^p$ convex on $[0, \infty)$.
Finiteness makes the total weight $W$ a finite positive number.

steps.slogan: Normalize the weights to probabilities $\pi_i = w_i/W$.
steps.detail: Let $W = \sum_i w_i > 0$. The numbers $\pi_i = w_i/W$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$, so $\sum_i \pi_i f_i$ is a [weighted mean](c:weighted-mean) of the $f_i$.

steps.slogan: Apply Jensen's inequality to the [convex function](c:convex-function) $t \mapsto t^p$.
steps.detail: For $p \ge 1$ the function $t^p$ is convex on $[0, \infty)$. Jensen's inequality gives $\bigl(\sum_i \pi_i f_i\bigr)^p \le \sum_i \pi_i f_i^p$.

steps.slogan: Clear the denominators and take the $p$-th root of both sides.
steps.detail: Multiplying by $W^p$ gives $\bigl(\sum_i w_i f_i\bigr)^p \le W^{p-1}\sum_i w_i f_i^p$. Both sides are nonnegative, so taking $p$-th roots gives $\sum_i w_i f_i \le W^{1-1/p}\bigl(\sum_i w_i f_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}$.

concepts.c:weighted-sum: The inequality bounds this weighted sum by a power mean.
concepts.c:finite-sum: All sums are finite, so the normalizing total $W$ is a real number.
concepts.c:weighted-mean: The normalized sum is the mean that Jensen's inequality compares.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of $t^p$ is the one analytic fact that the proof needs.

source.note: The standard derivation of Hölder-type inequalities from Jensen's inequality, as in Hardy, Littlewood and Pólya, Inequalities, chapter 2.

statement: Let $T^k_q$ be a [tensor operator](c:tensor-operator) of rank $k$ for [SU(2)](c:su-2), and $|j\,m\rangle$, $|j'\,m'\rangle$ standard basis vectors of irreducible representations. Then $\langle j\,m|T^k_q|j'\,m'\rangle = \langle j'\,m';k\,q|j\,m\rangle\,\langle j\|T^k\|j'\rangle$: a [Clebsch-Gordan coefficient](c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient) times a reduced element independent of $m, m', q$.

hypotheses.text: The operators $T^k_q$ form a [tensor operator](c:tensor-operator) of rank $k$: they transform under $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ like the basis $|k\,q\rangle$ of the spin-$k$ representation.
The vectors $|j\,m\rangle$ and $|j'\,m'\rangle$ are standard basis vectors of [irreducible representations](c:irreducible-representation) of spins $j$ and $j'$ inside one unitary representation.

conclusion: The matrix element is a [Clebsch-Gordan coefficient](c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient) times a number independent of $m, m', q$; it vanishes unless $m = m' + q$ and $|k - j'| \le j \le k + j'$.

proofs.name: Equivariant map and Schur's lemma
proofs.slogan: Read the tensor operator as an equivariant map out of $V_k \otimes V_{j'}$, so that Schur's lemma leaves one free number.
proofs.scope: Spin representations $V_j$ with the standard phase convention; another sign convention for the Clebsch-Gordan coefficient changes only a factor $(-1)^{k+j'-j}$ inside the reduced element. The same proof works for $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ with integer spins.

roles.why: The transformation law of $T^k_q$ is exactly the equivariance of the map $\Phi$.
The states span invariant subspaces $V_j$ and $V_{j'}$, which allows the projection and Schur's lemma.

steps.slogan: Package the tensor operator as an equivariant map $\Phi\colon V_k \otimes V_{j'} \to H$.
steps.detail: Define $\Phi(|k\,q\rangle \otimes |j'\,m'\rangle) = T^k_q|j'\,m'\rangle$. The tensor law $U T^k_q U^{-1} = \sum_{q'} D^k_{q'q}\,T^k_{q'}$, together with $U|j'\,m'\rangle = \sum_{m''} D^{j'}_{m''m'}|j'\,m''\rangle$, gives $U\,\Phi(v \otimes w) = \Phi(gv \otimes gw)$. So $\Phi$ is equivariant.

steps.slogan: Project onto the invariant subspace $V_j$ to get an equivariant map into $V_j$.
steps.detail: The orthogonal projection $P_j$ onto $V_j$ commutes with the unitary action. So $\Psi = P_j \circ \Phi\colon V_k \otimes V_{j'} \to V_j$ is equivariant, and $\langle j\,m|\Psi(|k\,q\rangle \otimes |j'\,m'\rangle) = \langle j\,m|T^k_q|j'\,m'\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Decompose $V_k \otimes V_{j'}$ into spins and count the equivariant maps into $V_j$.
steps.detail: Clebsch-Gordan theory gives $V_k \otimes V_{j'} \cong \bigoplus_{J=|k-j'|}^{k+j'} V_J$, each spin occurring once. By Schur's lemma the equivariant maps into the [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) $V_j$ form a space of dimension $1$ if $j$ occurs and $0$ otherwise.

steps.slogan: Identify $\Psi$ as a multiple of the Clebsch-Gordan projection and read off the matrix elements.
steps.detail: If $j$ does not occur, then $\Psi = 0$ and every matrix element vanishes. Otherwise $\Psi = c\,\pi_j$, where $\pi_j$ projects onto the copy of $V_j$ and has the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients as matrix elements, which vanish unless $m = m' + q$. So the matrix element is $c$ times a coefficient, and $c$ does not depend on $m, m', q$.

concepts.c:tensor-operator: Its transformation law is the equivariance that Schur's lemma exploits.
concepts.c:su-2: The group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ acts on all spaces and its irreducibles are the spins $V_j$.
concepts.c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient: These coefficients are the matrix elements of the unique equivariant projection.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility of $V_j$ lets Schur's lemma limit the equivariant maps.

source.note: The representation-theoretic form of the argument in Sakurai and Napolitano, Modern Quantum Mechanics, chapter 3 (tensor operators and the Wigner-Eckart theorem).

statement: For an integer $n > 1$, the [factorial](c:factorial) satisfies $(n-1)! \equiv -1$ in [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic) modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).

hypotheses.text: The integer $n$ satisfies $n > 1$.

conclusion: The number $n$ divides $(n-1)! + 1$ exactly when $n$ is prime.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the forward direction: $(p-1)! = -1$ in $\mathbb Z/p$ for a prime $p$. The converse is Nat.prime_of_fac_equiv_neg_one, and Nat.prime_iff_fac_equiv_neg_one joins both.

proofs.name: Pairing units with inverses
proofs.slogan: Multiply all nonzero residues modulo a prime in inverse pairs, and rule out composite numbers with a proper divisor.
proofs.scope: Both directions for every $n > 1$; the prime $p = 2$ is handled in step 3. A composite $n$ has a divisor $a$ with $1 < a < n$.

roles.why: For $n > 1$ the number $n$ is either prime or has a divisor $a$ with $1 < a < n$.

steps.slogan: Identify $(p-1)!$ with the product of all units of $\mathbb Z/p$ for a prime $p$.
steps.detail: For a prime $p$, the ring $\mathbb Z/p$ is a [field](c:field), so its nonzero elements $1, \dots, p-1$ are exactly its [units](c:group-of-units). Hence $(p-1)! = \prod_{x \in (\mathbb Z/p)^\times} x$.

steps.slogan: Pair each unit $x$ with its inverse $x^{-1}$.
steps.detail: A unit equals its inverse exactly when $x^2 = 1$, that is $(x-1)(x+1) = 0$. A field has no zero divisors, so $x = \pm 1$. The other units split into pairs $\{x, x^{-1}\}$ whose product is $1$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the pairs to find that the product of all units is $-1$.
steps.detail: The pairs contribute $1$. For odd $p$ the units $1$ and $-1$ are distinct, so the product is $1 \cdot (-1) = -1$. For $p = 2$ the only unit is $1 = -1$. So $(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod p$.

steps.slogan: Show that a composite $n$ does not satisfy the congruence.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be a divisor of $n$ with $1 < a < n$. Then $a$ is a factor of $(n-1)!$. If $n \mid (n-1)! + 1$, then $a \mid (n-1)! + 1$, so $a \mid 1$, which is false.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases into the equivalence for every $n > 1$.
steps.detail: A prime satisfies the congruence by steps 1 to 3, and a composite number does not by step 4. Every $n > 1$ is one of the two, so the congruence holds if and only if $n$ is prime.

concepts.c:factorial: The product $(n-1)!$ is the quantity that the congruence evaluates.
concepts.c:modular-arithmetic: The theorem is a statement about residues modulo $n$.
concepts.c:prime-number: Primality makes $\mathbb Z/n$ a field and rules out proper divisors.
concepts.c:field: A field has no zero divisors, so only $\pm 1$ are self-inverse.
concepts.c:group-of-units: The nonzero residues form the unit group, which inversion pairs up.

source.note: mathlib matches $1, \dots, p-1$ with the units of ZMod p and uses prod_univ_units_id_eq_neg_one (pair each unit with its inverse); the converse is Nat.prime_of_fac_equiv_neg_one.

proofs.name: Factoring $X^{p-1} - 1$
proofs.slogan: Factor $X^{p-1} - 1$ over the field $\mathbb Z/p$ into linear factors and compare constant terms.
proofs.scope: Both directions for every $n > 1$. The prime case uses a polynomial identity; the composite case is the divisor argument.

roles.why: For $n > 1$ the number $n$ is either prime or has a divisor $a$ with $1 < a < n$.

steps.slogan: Show that each of $1, \dots, p-1$ is a root of $X^{p-1} - 1$ in $\mathbb Z/p$.
steps.detail: For a prime $p$ and $a \not\equiv 0$, Fermat's little theorem gives $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. So the $p-1$ distinct residues $1, \dots, p-1$ are roots of $X^{p-1} - 1$.

steps.slogan: Factor the polynomial completely over the [field](c:field) $\mathbb Z/p$.
steps.detail: A polynomial of degree $p-1$ over a field has at most $p-1$ roots, and each root gives a linear factor. The monic polynomial $X^{p-1} - 1$ therefore equals $\prod_{a=1}^{p-1}(X - a)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the constant terms of the two sides.
steps.detail: Set $X = 0$ to get $-1 = (-1)^{p-1}(p-1)!$. For odd $p$ the sign $(-1)^{p-1}$ is $1$, so $(p-1)! \equiv -1$. For $p = 2$, $1! = 1 \equiv -1 \pmod 2$.

steps.slogan: Show that a composite $n$ does not satisfy the congruence.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be a divisor of $n$ with $1 < a < n$. Then $a \mid (n-1)!$. If $n \mid (n-1)! + 1$, then $a \mid 1$, which is false.

steps.slogan: Combine the prime and composite cases into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Primes satisfy the congruence by the first three steps and composite numbers do not by the fourth. Every $n > 1$ is prime or composite, so the equivalence holds.

concepts.c:factorial: The product $(n-1)!$ is the quantity that the congruence evaluates.
concepts.c:modular-arithmetic: The theorem is a statement about residues modulo $n$.
concepts.c:prime-number: Primality makes $\mathbb Z/n$ a field and rules out proper divisors.
concepts.c:field: Over a field, a polynomial has at most as many roots as its degree.

source.note: The classical proof that compares $X^{p-1} - 1$ with $\prod (X - a)$, as in Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, chapter 6.

statement: Let $F$ be an [endofunctor](c:endofunctor) of a category with an [initial object](c:initial-object) $0$. If the chain $0 \to F0 \to F^2 0 \to \cdots$ has a [colimit](c:colimit) $I$ that $F$ preserves, then $F$ has an [initial algebra](c:initial-algebra) with carrier $I$.

hypotheses.text: The category has an [initial object](c:initial-object) $0$.
The chain $0 \xrightarrow{!} F0 \xrightarrow{F!} F^2 0 \to \cdots$ has a [colimit](c:colimit) $I$ with injections $\iota_n\colon F^n 0 \to I$.
The functor $F$ preserves this colimit: the cocone $(F\iota_n)_n$ is a colimit of $F$ applied to the chain.

conclusion: There is an isomorphism $a\colon FI \to I$, and $(I, a)$ is an initial $F$-algebra.

proofs.name: Iterating the functor on the initial object
proofs.slogan: Take the colimit of the initial chain, use preservation to get the structure map, and build the unique algebra morphism from the chain.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for an arbitrary category with the three hypotheses. Algebras are pairs $(A, \alpha\colon FA \to A)$ and morphisms commute with the structure maps.

roles.why: The unique map out of $0$ starts the chain and starts the recursion for the maps $h_n$.
The colimit $I$ with its injections is the candidate carrier of the initial algebra.
Preservation identifies $FI$ with $I$ and makes the maps $F\iota_n$ jointly epimorphic.

steps.slogan: Build the initial chain and name its colimit $I$ with injections $\iota_n$.
steps.detail: Let $c_0 = {!}\colon 0 \to F0$ and $c_{n+1} = F c_n$, so the chain is $F^n 0 \xrightarrow{c_n} F^{n+1} 0$. Its [colimit](c:colimit) $I$ has injections $\iota_n$ with $\iota_{n+1} c_n = \iota_n$.

steps.slogan: Get the structure map $a\colon FI \to I$ from the preservation of the colimit.
steps.detail: By preservation, $(F\iota_n)$ is a colimit of the chain $F^{n+1}0$. The cocone $(\iota_{n+1})$ is also a colimit of that chain, because dropping the first term of a chain does not change its colimit. So a unique isomorphism $a$ has $a\,F\iota_n = \iota_{n+1}$.

steps.slogan: For a given algebra $(A, \alpha)$, define maps $h_n\colon F^n 0 \to A$ by recursion.
steps.detail: Let $h_0$ be the unique map $0 \to A$ and $h_{n+1} = \alpha\,F h_n$. Then $h_{n+1}c_n = h_n$ by induction: the base case holds since $0$ is initial, and $h_{n+2}c_{n+1} = \alpha F(h_{n+1}c_n) = \alpha F h_n = h_{n+1}$. So $(h_n)$ is a [cocone](c:cocone) on the chain.

steps.slogan: Induce $h\colon I \to A$ and check that it is an algebra morphism.
steps.detail: The cocone gives $h$ with $h\iota_n = h_n$. Then $h\,a\,F\iota_n = h\iota_{n+1} = h_{n+1} = \alpha\,F h_n = \alpha\,F h\,F\iota_n$. The maps $F\iota_n$ are jointly epimorphic, so $h\,a = \alpha\,F h$.

steps.slogan: Show that every algebra morphism $g\colon I \to A$ equals $h$, so $(I, a)$ is initial.
steps.detail: Suppose $g\,a = \alpha\,F g$. Then $g\iota_0 = h_0$ since $0$ is initial, and $g\iota_{n+1} = g\,a\,F\iota_n = \alpha\,F(g\iota_n) = \alpha\,F h_n = h_{n+1}$. So $g\iota_n = h\iota_n$ for all $n$, and the colimit property gives $g = h$.

concepts.c:endofunctor: The functor $F$ is iterated on $0$ and acts on the algebra structure.
concepts.c:initial-object: Initiality of $0$ gives the first map of the chain and the base cases.
concepts.c:colimit: The colimit of the chain is the carrier, and its universal property gives $h$ and $g = h$.
concepts.c:initial-algebra: The goal is an algebra with exactly one morphism to every algebra.
concepts.c:cocone: The maps $h_n$ form a cocone, which induces the algebra morphism.

source.note: J. Adámek, Free algebras and automata realizations in the language of categories, Commentationes Mathematicae Universitatis Carolinae 15 (1974); see also the nLab entry on Adámek's fixed point theorem.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonempty proper subset of the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$ that is a [finite CW complex](c:finite-cw-complex). Then $\tilde H_i(S^n \setminus X) \cong \check H^{\,n-i-1}(X)$ for every integer $i$, with the [reduced homology](c:reduced-homology) of the complement and reduced [Čech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) of $X$.

hypotheses.text: The subset $X$ is a [finite CW complex](c:finite-cw-complex).
The subset $X$ is nonempty and different from $S^n$.

conclusion: The reduced homology of the complement equals the reduced Čech cohomology of $X$ with the degree shift $i \mapsto n-i-1$.

proofs.name: Duality for compact subsets of a sphere
proofs.slogan: Pass to the homology of the pair $(S^n, S^n \setminus X)$, identify it with the cohomology of $X$ by duality on neighbourhoods, and fix the extreme degrees.
proofs.scope: An outline: the duality of step 2 for compact locally contractible subsets of a closed orientable manifold rests on the cited work. The case $n = 1$ is included.

roles.why: A finite complex is compact and locally contractible, and its Čech and singular cohomology agree.
Nonemptiness gives reduced cohomology, and properness keeps the complement from being empty.

steps.slogan: Replace the complement by the pair $(S^n, S^n \setminus X)$ in the long exact sequence.
steps.detail: The [long exact sequence](c:long-exact-sequence-in-chain-homology) of the pair in reduced homology contains $\tilde H_{i+1}(S^n) \to H_{i+1}(S^n, S^n \setminus X) \to \tilde H_i(S^n \setminus X) \to \tilde H_i(S^n)$. The groups $\tilde H_*(S^n)$ vanish outside degree $n$, so $\tilde H_i(S^n \setminus X) \cong H_{i+1}(S^n, S^n \setminus X)$ for $i \ne n-1, n$.

steps.slogan: Identify the relative homology of the pair with the cohomology of $X$ by duality.
steps.detail: For a compact, [locally contractible](c:locally-contractible-space) subset $X$ of a closed [orientable manifold](c:orientable-manifold) such as $S^n$, one has $H_j(S^n, S^n \setminus X) \cong H^{n-j}(X)$. The proof applies Poincaré duality to neighbourhoods of $X$ and passes to the limit.

steps.slogan: Assemble all degrees and treat the two extreme degrees separately.
steps.detail: For $i \ne n-1, n$, steps 1 and 2 give $\tilde H_i(S^n \setminus X) \cong H^{n-i-1}(X)$. For $i = n-1$ the exact sequence ends in $H_n(S^n) \to H^0(X) \to \tilde H_{n-1}(S^n \setminus X) \to 0$, whose cokernel is $\tilde H^0(X)$ after comparing with a point of $X$. For $i \ge n$ both sides vanish.

steps.slogan: Replace singular by [Čech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) for the finite complex $X$.
steps.detail: A finite CW complex is compact and locally contractible, so its Čech and singular cohomology agree. Hence $\tilde H_i(S^n \setminus X) \cong \check H^{\,n-i-1}(X)$ in every degree $i$.

concepts.c:sphere: The ambient sphere is a closed orientable manifold with simple homology.
concepts.c:finite-cw-complex: Finiteness gives compactness and local contractibility, which the duality needs.
concepts.c:reduced-homology: Reduced groups make the sphere's homology vanish outside degree $n$.
concepts.c:cech-cohomology: Čech cohomology of $X$ is the right-hand side of the duality.
concepts.c:long-exact-sequence-in-chain-homology: The sequence of the pair links the complement to the relative groups.
concepts.c:locally-contractible-space: Local contractibility lets cohomology of $X$ be computed from neighbourhoods.
concepts.c:orientable-manifold: Poincaré duality needs an orientable closed manifold, here $S^n$.

source.ref: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, Theorem 3.44 (Alexander duality), section 3.3
source.note: Hatcher proves the isomorphism for compact, locally contractible, nonempty proper subsets of $S^n$; the outline follows his reduction to the duality for compact subsets of a closed orientable manifold.

statement: For $n \ge 5$ the [alternating group](c:alternating-group) $A_n$ is a [simple group](c:simple-group): its only [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) are the trivial group and $A_n$.

hypotheses.text: The degree satisfies $n \ge 5$.

conclusion: The group $A_n$ is nontrivial, and every normal subgroup of $A_n$ is trivial or equal to $A_n$.

proofs.name: Iwasawa criterion on 3-subsets
proofs.slogan: Let the group act primitively on 3-subsets, so that a normal subgroup is transitive and the quotient is abelian, then use perfectness.
proofs.scope: Degrees $n \ge 5$ with $n \ne 6$. For $n = 6$ mathlib runs the same steps on 4-subsets with Klein four-groups; the second proof covers every $n \ge 5$.

roles.why: Degree at least $5$ gives outside points for commutators, faithfulness and the block argument; $n \ne 6$ is used for primitivity.

steps.slogan: Show that $A_n$ equals its commutator subgroup.
steps.detail: For a 3-cycle $(a\,b\,c)$ pick $d, e \notin \{a, b, c\}$, which is possible as $n \ge 5$. Then $(a\,b\,c) = [(b\,c\,d), (a\,e\,b)]$ is a [commutator](c:commutator) of even permutations, with $[x,y] = xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$. Since 3-cycles generate $A_n$, the group is [perfect](c:is-perfect).

steps.slogan: Let $G = A_n$ act on the 3-subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and name the subgroups $T_s$.
steps.detail: The action is transitive, since an odd permutation can be fixed by a transposition inside the target set, and it is faithful as $n \ge 5$. For a 3-subset $s$ let $T_s$ be the even permutations supported in $s$: cyclic of order $3$ and normal in the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) $G_s$. The conjugates of the $T_s$ contain all 3-cycles, so they generate $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that the action on 3-subsets is [primitive](c:is-preprimitive) when $n \ne 6$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be a block with $s \in B$ and another $t \in B$. Elements fixing $s$ preserve $B$, and they are transitive on the 3-subsets sharing two points with $s$; so if $|s \cap t| = 2$, chaining through such neighbours gives $B = X$. If $|s \cap t| = 1$, a 3-cycle of $T_s$ moves $t$ to a neighbour of $t$ in $B$. If $s \cap t = \emptyset$, then $n \ge 7$ and a 3-cycle on two points of $t$ and one outside point does the same.

steps.slogan: Show that a nontrivial normal subgroup $N$ is transitive on the 3-subsets.
steps.detail: Since $N$ is normal, $g$ maps an $N$-orbit to an $N$-orbit, so the orbits are blocks. The action is faithful, so $N \ne 1$ moves some $s$ and its [orbit](c:orbit) has at least two elements. By primitivity this orbit is the whole set.

steps.slogan: Show that $G/N$ is generated by the image of the abelian group $T_s$.
steps.detail: Transitivity gives $G = N G_s$. For $g = nh$ with $n \in N$ and $h \in G_s$, the group $hT_sh^{-1} = T_s$, so $gT_sg^{-1}$ and $T_s$ have the same image in $G/N$. The conjugates of $T_s$ generate $G$, so the image of $T_s$ generates $G/N$, which is therefore abelian.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $N = G$, because $G$ equals its commutator subgroup.
steps.detail: An abelian quotient $G/N$ means that $N$ contains the commutator subgroup $[G, G]$. By step 1, $[G, G] = G$, so $N = G$. As $A_n \ne 1$, the group is simple, following the [Iwasawa criterion](c:iwasawa-structure).

concepts.c:alternating-group: The group $G = A_n$ is the group that the proof shows to be simple.
concepts.c:simple-group: Simplicity is the goal: no normal subgroup other than $1$ and $G$.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality makes orbits into blocks and lets conjugation act on the quotient.
concepts.c:commutator: Commutators show that the group is perfect and that abelian quotients are trivial.
concepts.c:is-perfect: A perfect group has no nontrivial abelian quotient.
concepts.c:stabilizer: The stabilizer $G_s$ normalizes $T_s$ and gives $G = N G_s$.
concepts.c:is-preprimitive: Primitivity forces an orbit of $N$ with two points to be everything.
concepts.c:orbit: The orbits of $N$ are blocks of the action.
concepts.c:iwasawa-structure: The family $T_s$ with these properties is an Iwasawa structure.

source.note: mathlib applies the Iwasawa criterion (IwasawaStructure.commutator_le) to the preprimitive action on 3-subsets (iwasawaStructure_three), and on 4-subsets when the degree is 6.

proofs.name: Three-cycles in a normal subgroup
proofs.slogan: Show that a nontrivial normal subgroup contains a 3-cycle by a case split on cycle types, then that 3-cycles are conjugate and generate.
proofs.scope: Every degree $n \ge 5$. The case split on the cycle type of one nonidentity element covers all possibilities.

roles.why: Degree at least $5$ supplies the extra points used in the conjugation step and in the transposition case.

steps.slogan: Show that 3-cycles generate $A_n$.
steps.detail: Every even permutation is a product of an even number of transpositions. Two transpositions with a common point give a [3-cycle](c:3-cycle), as $(a\,b)(a\,c) = (a\,c\,b)$. Two disjoint ones give $(a\,b)(c\,d) = (a\,c\,b)(a\,c\,d)$, a product of two 3-cycles.

steps.slogan: Show that all 3-cycles are conjugate in $A_n$ when $n \ge 5$.
steps.detail: In $S_n$, any two 3-cycles are [conjugate](c:conjugacy-class): $g(a\,b\,c)g^{-1} = (a'\,b'\,c')$. If $g$ is odd, replace it by $g(d\,e)$ with $d, e \notin \{a, b, c\}$. The transposition $(d\,e)$ commutes with $(a\,b\,c)$, so the new element conjugates the same way and is even.

steps.slogan: Find a 3-cycle in $N$ from an element with a long cycle or two 3-cycles.
steps.detail: Let $1 \ne \sigma \in N$. If $\sigma = (a_1\,a_2\,\dots\,a_r)\tau$ with $r \ge 4$, then with $\delta = (a_1\,a_2\,a_3)$ the [commutator](c:commutator) $\delta\sigma\delta^{-1}\sigma^{-1} \in N$ equals $(a_1\,a_2\,a_4)$. If $\sigma = (1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6)\tau$ and $\delta = (1\,2\,4)$, the commutator is a 5-cycle, which falls under the first case.

steps.slogan: Find a 3-cycle in $N$ from an element with one 3-cycle or only transpositions.
steps.detail: If $\sigma = (1\,2\,3)\tau$ with $\tau$ a product of disjoint transpositions, then $\sigma^2 = (1\,3\,2) \in N$. If $\sigma = (1\,2)(3\,4)\tau$ with $\tau$ such a product, then $\pi = [(1\,2\,3), \sigma] = (1\,3)(2\,4) \in N$, and $\pi \cdot (1\,3\,5)\pi(1\,3\,5)^{-1} = (1\,3\,5) \in N$.

steps.slogan: Collect the cases to put a 3-cycle in $N$, then conclude that $N = A_n$.
steps.detail: A nonidentity $\sigma$ has a cycle of length at least four, or at least two 3-cycles, or exactly one 3-cycle, or none. In each case $N$ contains a 3-cycle, hence all 3-cycles by step 2, hence $N = A_n$ by step 1. Since $A_n \ne 1$, it is simple.

concepts.c:alternating-group: The proof describes the even permutations through 3-cycles.
concepts.c:simple-group: Simplicity means that a nontrivial normal subgroup must be the whole group.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality puts commutators with a 3-cycle back inside $N$.
concepts.c:3-cycle: The 3-cycles generate $A_n$ and form a single conjugacy class.
concepts.c:conjugacy-class: One conjugacy class of 3-cycles spreads a single 3-cycle in $N$ to all.
concepts.c:commutator: Commutators of an element of $N$ with a 3-cycle stay in $N$ and are short cycles.

source.note: The classical argument on cycle types, as in Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra, section 4.6.

statement: The [series](c:series) $\sum_{n \ge 1} 1/n^2$ converges and equals $\pi^2/6$; equivalently $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ for the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function).

formal.difference: The declaration sums over all natural numbers, with the term at $n = 0$ equal to $0$ because division by zero is $0$ in Lean. It is the case $k = 1$ of the general formula hasSum_zeta_nat.

proofs.name: Fourier series of a Bernoulli polynomial
proofs.slogan: Expand the periodic quadratic $x^2 - x + 1/6$ in a Fourier series and evaluate the series at $x = 0$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity, with no hypotheses. The expansion is a pointwise equality at every $x$, including $x = 0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the Fourier coefficients of the periodic function $B(x) = x^2 - x + 1/6$.
steps.detail: Extend the [Bernoulli polynomial](c:bernoulli-polynomial) $B$ from $[0, 1)$ to a $1$-[periodic function](c:periodic-function); it is continuous because $B(0) = B(1)$. Two integrations by parts give $\hat B(0) = 0$ and $\hat B(n) = \int_0^1 B(x)e^{-2\pi i n x}\,dx = \frac{1}{2\pi^2 n^2}$ for $n \neq 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Fourier coefficients are absolutely summable.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 2$ we have $1/n^2 \le \frac1{n-1} - \frac1n$, and the right sides telescope. So $\sum_{n \ge 1} 1/n^2 \le 2$, and $\sum_{n \in \mathbb Z}|\hat B(n)|$ converges.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) of $B$ converges to $B$ at every point.
steps.detail: A series with absolutely summable coefficients converges uniformly to a continuous function $g$ with the same coefficients. The continuous function $B - g$ has all Fourier coefficients zero, so it vanishes by the uniqueness theorem. Hence $B(x) = \sum_n \hat B(n)e^{2\pi i n x}$ for every $x$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the expansion at $x = 0$ to read off the sum.
steps.detail: At $x = 0$ we get $\frac16 = B(0) = \sum_{n \ne 0}\frac{1}{2\pi^2 n^2} = \frac{1}{\pi^2}\sum_{n \ge 1}\frac{1}{n^2}$. Multiplying by $\pi^2$ gives $\sum_{n \ge 1} 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$.

concepts.c:series: The theorem is the value of this series.
concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: The sum is the value of the zeta function at $2$.
concepts.c:bernoulli-polynomial: The quadratic $B$ is the second Bernoulli polynomial, with a simple Fourier series.
concepts.c:periodic-function: Periodic extension makes $B$ a continuous function on the circle.
concepts.c:fourier-series: The Fourier series of $B$ at $0$ is the series $\sum 1/n^2$ up to a factor.

source.note: mathlib specializes hasSum_zeta_nat, which evaluates the Fourier series of the periodized Bernoulli polynomial at $x = 0$ (hasSum_one_div_nat_pow_mul_cos), with $B_2 = 1/6$.

statement: Let $A = VDV^{-1}$ be a [diagonalizable matrix](c:diagonalizable-matrix) with $D = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m)$, let $\|\cdot\|$ be an induced $p$-[matrix norm](c:matrix-norm), and let $E$ be any matrix. If $\mu$ is an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $A + E$, then $\min_i |\mu - \lambda_i| \le \kappa(V)\,\|E\|$, where $\kappa(V) = \|V\|\,\|V^{-1}\|$ is the [condition number](c:condition-number).

hypotheses.text: The matrix factors as $A = VDV^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal, so $A$ is [diagonalizable](c:diagonalizable-matrix).
The norm is an induced $p$-[matrix norm](c:matrix-norm) with $1 \le p \le \infty$, so it is submultiplicative and $\|D\| = \max_i |d_i|$ for diagonal $D$.
The number $\mu$ is an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $A + E$ for a square matrix $E$ of the same size.

proofs.name: Resolvent bound
proofs.slogan: Rewrite the eigenvector equation of $A + E$ in the eigenbasis of $A$, invert $\mu I - D$ and take norms.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The case that $\mu$ is already an eigenvalue of $A$ is immediate and is treated first.

roles.why: It gives a nonzero vector $x$ with $(A + E)x = \mu x$.
The factorization turns $\mu I - A$ into $V(\mu I - D)V^{-1}$ with a diagonal middle factor.
Submultiplicativity bounds the product of norms, and the diagonal norm is the largest entry.

steps.slogan: Dispose of the case that $\mu$ equals an eigenvalue of $A$.
steps.detail: If $\mu = \lambda_i$ for some $i$, then $|\mu - \lambda_i| = 0 \le \kappa(V)\|E\|$ and the claim holds. Otherwise $\mu \ne \lambda_i$ for all $i$, so the diagonal matrix $\mu I - D$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Turn the eigenvector equation of $A + E$ into an equation for $w = V^{-1}x$.
steps.detail: Let $(A + E)x = \mu x$ with $x \ne 0$. Then $(\mu I - A)x = Ex$. With $A = VDV^{-1}$ and multiplication by $V^{-1}$ this becomes $(\mu I - D)w = (V^{-1}EV)\,w$, where $w = V^{-1}x \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Invert $\mu I - D$ and take norms to bound $1$ from above.
steps.detail: We have $w = (\mu I - D)^{-1}(V^{-1}EV)\,w$. Taking norms and using submultiplicativity gives $\|w\| \le \|(\mu I - D)^{-1}\|\,\|V^{-1}\|\,\|E\|\,\|V\|\,\|w\|$. Since $w \ne 0$, we get $1 \le \|(\mu I - D)^{-1}\|\,\kappa(V)\,\|E\|$.

steps.slogan: Compute the norm of the diagonal matrix $(\mu I - D)^{-1}$.
steps.detail: The induced $p$-norm of a diagonal matrix is its largest absolute entry. So $\|(\mu I - D)^{-1}\| = \max_i \frac{1}{|\mu - \lambda_i|} = \frac{1}{\min_i |\mu - \lambda_i|}$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two estimates to bound the distance to the nearest eigenvalue.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $1 \le \kappa(V)\,\|E\| / \min_i |\mu - \lambda_i|$. Hence $\min_i |\mu - \lambda_i| \le \kappa(V)\,\|E\|$.

concepts.c:diagonalizable-matrix: A diagonalizing factorization turns the problem into one about a diagonal matrix.
concepts.c:matrix-norm: Submultiplicativity and the diagonal norm formula give the estimate.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The perturbed eigenvalue $\mu$ supplies the eigenvector equation.
concepts.c:condition-number: The product $\|V\|\|V^{-1}\|$ appears as the factor in the bound.

source.note: The standard resolvent argument of F. L. Bauer and C. T. Fike, Norms and exclusion theorems, Numerische Mathematik 2 (1960).

statement: Let $\Lambda$ be a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) in $\mathbb R^n$ with a measurable [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) $F$, and let $S \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be measurable with $\mathrm{vol}(S) > \mathrm{vol}(F)$. Then $S$ contains two distinct points $s, t$ with $s - t \in \Lambda$.

hypotheses.text: The group $\Lambda$ is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) in $\mathbb R^n$ with a measurable [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) $F$ of finite volume.
The set $S$ is [measurable](c:measurable-set).
The volume of $S$ exceeds the covolume: $\mathrm{vol}(S) > \mathrm{vol}(F)$.

conclusion: Some distinct $s, t \in S$ have $s - t \in \Lambda$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for a countable group acting on a measure space with an invariant measure and a fundamental domain. It concludes that two translates $x + S$ and $y + S$, for distinct $x, y$, intersect; in $\mathbb R^n$ an intersection point gives two points of $S$ with difference $y - x \in \Lambda$.

proofs.name: Translate the pieces back
proofs.slogan: Cut $S$ along the translates of $F$, move every piece back into $F$, and note that pieces of total volume above $\mathrm{vol}(F)$ must overlap.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any lattice and any measurable $S$ with $\mathrm{vol}(S) > \mathrm{vol}(F)$, including $\mathrm{vol}(S) = \infty$. The two points are $z + \lambda$ and $z + \lambda'$ for a point $z$ of the overlap.

roles.why: The translates $\lambda + F$ tile the space, and the lattice is countable.
Measurability makes the volumes of the pieces defined and additive.
The excess volume forces the pieces inside $F$ to overlap.

steps.slogan: Cut $S$ along the translates of the [fundamental domain](c:fundamental-domain) $F$.
steps.detail: The translates $\lambda + F$ with $\lambda \in \Lambda$ cover $\mathbb R^n$ and overlap only in null sets, and $\Lambda$ is countable. So $\mathrm{vol}(S) = \sum_{\lambda \in \Lambda} \mathrm{vol}\bigl(S \cap (\lambda + F)\bigr)$.

steps.slogan: Translate each piece back into $F$ without changing its volume.
steps.detail: Put $S_\lambda = (S - \lambda) \cap F$. Translation preserves [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure), so $\mathrm{vol}(S_\lambda) = \mathrm{vol}(S \cap (\lambda + F))$. Hence $\sum_\lambda \mathrm{vol}(S_\lambda) = \mathrm{vol}(S) > \mathrm{vol}(F)$.

steps.slogan: Show that two of the pieces $S_\lambda$ share a point.
steps.detail: All $S_\lambda$ lie in $F$. If they were pairwise disjoint, countable additivity would give $\sum_\lambda \mathrm{vol}(S_\lambda) = \mathrm{vol}(\bigcup_\lambda S_\lambda) \le \mathrm{vol}(F)$, against step 2. So some $z$ lies in $S_\lambda \cap S_{\lambda'}$ with $\lambda \ne \lambda'$.

steps.slogan: Read off two points of $S$ whose difference is a lattice vector.
steps.detail: From $z \in S_\lambda \cap S_{\lambda'}$ we get $z + \lambda \in S$ and $z + \lambda' \in S$. These points are distinct, and their difference $\lambda - \lambda'$ lies in $\Lambda$.

concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: The lattice supplies the countable group of translations.
concepts.c:fundamental-domain: Its translates tile the space and give the pieces of $S$.
concepts.c:measurable-set: Measurability lets volumes of the pieces add up.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Translation invariance of volume keeps the volume of each moved piece.

source.note: mathlib argues by contraposition: if the translates of $S$ were pairwise disjoint, then $\mu(S) = \sum \mu((x + S) \cap F)$ (IsAddFundamentalDomain.measure_eq_tsum) is the measure of a disjoint union inside $F$ (measure_iUnion₀, measure_mono), hence at most $\mu(F)$.

statement: Let $B$ be a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra), $I$ an [ideal](c:ideal) of $B$ and $F$ a [filter](c:filter) of $B$ with $I \cap F = \emptyset$. Then some [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $J \supseteq I$ has $J \cap F = \emptyset$.

hypotheses.text: The structure $B$ is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra).
The set $I$ is an [ideal](c:ideal) and $F$ is a nonempty [filter](c:filter) of $B$.
The ideal and the filter are disjoint: $I \cap F = \emptyset$.

conclusion: There is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $J$ of $B$ with $I \subseteq J$ and $J \cap F = \emptyset$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds in any distributive lattice, not only in a Boolean algebra, and calls an ideal prime when its complement is a filter.

proofs.name: Maximal ideal by Zorn's lemma
proofs.slogan: Take an ideal that contains $I$, misses $F$ and is maximal for these properties, and show with distributivity that it is prime.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof uses the axiom of choice through Zorn's lemma, and it uses only the distributive law of $B$.

roles.why: It puts $I$ itself into the family of admissible ideals.
Unions of chains of ideals are ideals, and the filter is upward closed and closed under meets.
The distributive law lets the two meets of filter elements be compared with $a_1 \wedge a_2$.

steps.slogan: Collect the ideals that contain $I$ and miss $F$ into a poset $\mathcal S$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of ideals $K$ with $I \subseteq K$ and $K \cap F = \emptyset$, ordered by inclusion. By hypothesis $I \in \mathcal S$, so $\mathcal S$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Show that every nonempty chain in $\mathcal S$ has an upper bound in $\mathcal S$.
steps.detail: The union of a nonempty chain of ideals is a lower set, and it is directed because any two members lie in one ideal of the chain. It contains $I$ and misses $F$, since each member does. So the union lies in $\mathcal S$.

steps.slogan: Take a maximal element $J$ of $\mathcal S$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Every chain of $\mathcal S$ has an upper bound, so $\mathcal S$ has a maximal element $J$. It is proper, because $F$ is nonempty and upward closed, so it contains the top element $1$, which $J$ misses.

steps.slogan: Enlarge $J$ by an element outside it and use maximality to meet $F$.
steps.detail: Let $a_1, a_2 \notin J$ and let $J_i$ be the ideal generated by $J \cup \{a_i\}$, so $J_i \supsetneq J$. By maximality $J_i \notin \mathcal S$, so it meets $F$ (it contains $I$). Pick $c_i \in F$ with $c_i \le j_i \vee a_i$ for some $j_i \in J$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two filter elements to show that $a_1 \wedge a_2 \notin J$.
steps.detail: Put $j = j_1 \vee j_2 \in J$. Then $c_1 \wedge c_2 \in F$ and, by the [distributive law](c:distributive-lattice), $c_1 \wedge c_2 \le (j \vee a_1) \wedge (j \vee a_2) = j \vee (a_1 \wedge a_2)$, so this element lies in $F$. If $a_1 \wedge a_2 \in J$, it would lie in $J \cap F$, which is empty. So the complement of $J$ is closed under meets, and $J$ is prime.

concepts.c:boolean-algebra: The algebra is distributive, which the primality argument needs.
concepts.c:ideal: The admissible objects are ideals containing $I$; chains of them have unions.
concepts.c:filter: The filter is upward closed and closed under meets, which gives the contradiction.
concepts.c:prime-ideal: The maximal ideal is shown to be prime, which is the goal.
concepts.c:distributive-lattice: Distributivity turns $(j \vee a_1) \wedge (j \vee a_2)$ into $j \vee (a_1 \wedge a_2)$.

source.note: mathlib applies Zorn's lemma (zorn_subset_nonempty) to the ideals containing $I$ and disjoint from $F$, then proves a maximal one prime with the distributive law.

statement: For every family $(a_\alpha)$ of real numbers indexed by multi-indices $\alpha \in \mathbb N^m$ there is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f\colon \mathbb R^m \to \mathbb R$ with $\partial^\alpha f(0) = a_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$. So every formal [power series](c:power-series) is the [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) of a smooth function at $0$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $a_\alpha \in \mathbb R$ are arbitrary, one for each multi-index $\alpha \in \mathbb N^m$.

conclusion: A smooth function $f$ on $\mathbb R^m$ has $\partial^\alpha f(0) = a_\alpha$ for every multi-index $\alpha$.

proofs.name: Sum of cut-off monomials
proofs.slogan: Cut off each monomial at a scale so small that all its low-order derivatives are tiny, and add the cut-off monomials.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for any $m \ge 1$. The sum is over all multi-indices, enumerated by a fixed bijection $\alpha \mapsto m(\alpha)$ from $\mathbb N^m$ to $\mathbb N$.

roles.why: The numbers $a_\alpha$ are the coefficients of the monomials and set the size of each cut-off.

steps.slogan: Fix a [bump function](c:bump-function) $\chi$ equal to $1$ near the origin.
steps.detail: Choose a smooth $\chi\colon \mathbb R^m \to [0, 1]$ with $\chi = 1$ on $|x| \le 1/2$ and $\chi = 0$ for $|x| \ge 1$. All derivatives of $\chi$ are bounded.

steps.slogan: Form the terms $g_\alpha(x) = \frac{a_\alpha}{\alpha!}\,x^\alpha\,\chi(x/\varepsilon_\alpha)$ with scales $\varepsilon_\alpha \in (0, 1]$.
steps.detail: Near $0$ the cut-off equals $1$, so $g_\alpha(x) = \frac{a_\alpha}{\alpha!}x^\alpha$ there. Hence $\partial^\beta g_\alpha(0) = a_\alpha$ if $\beta = \alpha$ and $\partial^\beta g_\alpha(0) = 0$ if $\beta \ne \alpha$, whatever the scale $\varepsilon_\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Bound the derivatives of a term of lower order than its monomial by scaling.
steps.detail: Substituting $x = \varepsilon y$ gives $\sup|\partial^\beta(x^\alpha\chi(x/\varepsilon))| = \varepsilon^{|\alpha| - |\beta|}\sup|\partial^\beta(y^\alpha\chi)|$. Let $M_\alpha$ bound the right supremum for all $|\beta| < |\alpha|$. For $\varepsilon \le 1$ this gives $\sup|\partial^\beta g_\alpha| \le \varepsilon\,|a_\alpha|M_\alpha/\alpha!$.

steps.slogan: Choose each scale $\varepsilon_\alpha$ so that $\sup|\partial^\beta g_\alpha| \le 2^{-m(\alpha)}$ for all $|\beta| < |\alpha|$.
steps.detail: Take $\varepsilon_\alpha = \min\bigl(1, \; 2^{-m(\alpha)}\alpha!/((|a_\alpha| + 1)(M_\alpha + 1))\bigr)$. By the previous step, every derivative of order below $|\alpha|$ of $g_\alpha$ is then at most $2^{-m(\alpha)}$ in absolute value.

steps.slogan: Sum the terms and differentiate term by term to get a smooth function $f$.
steps.detail: Fix $\beta$. The terms with $|\alpha| > |\beta|$ have $\sup|\partial^\beta g_\alpha| \le 2^{-m(\alpha)}$, a summable bound, and the finitely many other terms are smooth. So $\sum_\alpha \partial^\beta g_\alpha$ converges [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) for every $\beta$. Hence $f = \sum_\alpha g_\alpha$ is smooth and $\partial^\beta f = \sum_\alpha \partial^\beta g_\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the derivatives of $f$ at the origin to find the prescribed numbers.
steps.detail: By the second step, $\partial^\beta g_\alpha(0)$ is $a_\beta$ for $\alpha = \beta$ and $0$ otherwise. So $\partial^\beta f(0) = \sum_\alpha \partial^\beta g_\alpha(0) = a_\beta$ for every multi-index $\beta$.

concepts.c:smooth-function: The constructed sum is smooth because every derivative series converges uniformly.
concepts.c:power-series: The prescribed numbers are the coefficients of an arbitrary formal power series.
concepts.c:taylor-series: The derivatives of $f$ at $0$ give the Taylor series of $f$.
concepts.c:bump-function: The cut-off function lets each monomial be switched off away from $0$.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence of each derivative series allows term-by-term differentiation.

source.note: The classical construction of É. Borel (1895): monomials cut off at shrinking scales so that every derivative series converges uniformly.
